# edubba-cuneiform-103 — one card per sign taught in the course, generated by

𒊭	<b>which</b> · ŠA · <i>[ša]</i> · the particle ša — "which, of"; the school's hinge-word<br>Which one? The one ša points at. Every time Akkadian glues a noun to a noun ("the lord — which is to say — of heaven") or hangs a clause on a noun ("the man who…"), this sign does the pointing. Learn one sign, own the language's hinge.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒅇	<b>and</b> · U3 · <i>[u]</i> · the conjunction u — "and"<br>And — the sign you'll meet exactly where English would put the word: between heaven and earth, the strong and the weak, silver and barley. When the line pauses to add one more thing, this is the wedge-cluster doing it.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒌝	<b>tether</b> · UM · <i>[um]</i> · [um]; the nominative's closing -um<br>A tether holds an animal to its post; -um tethers a noun to its role as subject. Spot this sign at a word's end and you know who the sentence is about — the noun is tied down, case settled.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒇷	<b>juniper</b> · LI · <i>[li/le]</i> · [li/le]; a juniper in the lists<br>A juniper is a modest tree with berries in everything — gin, stews, incense. The sign is the same: modest shape, spread through the whole corpus one li at a time. From chapter 08 it also carries the e-colored twin, le — the opener of lē'ûm, "the capable," the epilogue's word for its able king.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒅖	<b>dust</b> · IŠ · <i>[iš]</i> · dust, soil<br>Dust is what a foundation trench is dug through and what everything settles into. The sign starts at the bottom: where there is an iš, something is being grounded — a building's footing or a verb's past.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒅕	<b>scent</b> · IR · <i>[ir/er]</i> · scent, perfume in the lists<br>A scent drifts — you can't pin it to one spot, and this sign won't be pinned to one vowel. Catch the general direction (r, front vowel) and follow the word to its meaning.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒄠	<b>wild bull</b> · AM · <i>[am]</i> · wild bull — a bull-sign marked with "mountain"<br>The wild bull is what a sentence acts on at its peril — and -am marks the noun acted on. When a word ends in the bull, it is the object of the story: handle with care.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒁴	<b>post</b> · DIM · <i>[tim]</i> · post, pillar; the genitive's -tim<br>A post is what things are fastened to — and the genitive is the case of belonging. Where the post stands at a word's end, the word is tied to something: of the land, of the earth, of the year.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒍢	<b>bile</b> · ZE2 · <i>[ṣi/ṣe]</i> · bile, gall; the emphatic ṣ<br>Bile is sharp and it stings — so is the sound. When you see the bile-sign, press the s until it bites: ṣ, the consonant with an edge.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒁉	<b>its</b> · BI · <i>[pi]</i> · veteran — BI gains [pi₂]: the last syllable of Ḫammurapi<br>You know its voice already; now hear it pop. The proof it matters: the king of Babylon signs himself with it — Ḫa-am-mu-ra-pi₂ — and you cannot spell the most famous name in Mesopotamia without this veteran's new reading.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒁁	<b>open</b> · BAD · <i>[be]</i> · [be]; as a word, to open, apart<br>Open — the sign that opens doors opens titles: every bēlum, every "lord of…" begins by opening with be. One wedge apart, and the gates of rank swing wide.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒂖	<b>bright</b> · EL · <i>[el]</i> · bright, pure (ellum)<br>Bright — polished, cleared of tarnish. The sign finishes "lord" the way a shine finishes silver: be + el, and the title gleams.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒀜	<b>father</b> · AD · <i>[ad/at]</i> · father<br>The father stands at the head of the household and the end of the ledger: when a payment falls due in the laws — inaddin, "he shall pay" — the father-sign is right there in the middle of the word, holding the family accountable. The pressed third of the family, aṭ, arrives with the epilogue's šaṭram, "the inscribed" (chapter 18) — ad, at, aṭ: one sign, the whole dental row.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒅆	<b>eye</b> · IGI · <i>[ši/lim]</i> · veteran — IGI gains [ši/lim]: šīmātum's opener, awīlim's close<br>The eye goes abstract: what was watching is now just whispering ši. When destinies are decreed on the stele — šīmātum — the old eye opens the word without seeing a thing. And from chapter 10 the same sign carries a second syllable: lim, the closer of awīlim, "of a man" — every time the laws put a man in the genitive (a-wi-lim), the old eye seals the word. One sign, two workaday sounds, no eyes in either.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒌧	<b>the Land</b> · KALAM · <i>[mātum]</i> · veteran — KALAM gains [mātum]: the Land-sign as a sumerogram<br>Nothing to relearn: the sign still means the Land. Only the voice changes at the border — the eye reads Sumerian, the mouth answers in Akkadian. When you meet it in a reading, say mātum and move on.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒉣	<b>prince</b> · NUN · <i>[nun]</i> · prince, noble<br>A prince among syllables: it turns up where rank is being handed out. The gods who assign kingship on the stele's second line carry the prince-sign in their own family name.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒈗	<b>king</b> · LUGAL · <i>[šarrum]</i> · veteran — LUGAL gains [šarrum]: the king-sign as a sumerogram<br>The most royal sign in the school never changes its meaning, only its language. Where Sumerian said lugal, Babylon says šarrum — same wedges, new king.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒌒	<b>nook</b> · UB · <i>[ub]</i> · [ub]; a corner-nook in the lists<br>A nook is where things tuck in tight: the sign tucks in right behind the grass-sign in verb after verb, a snug -ub- pocket in the middle of the action.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒊌	<b>lion</b> · UG · <i>[ug/uk]</i> · a raging beast — a lion-sign marked with "day"<br>A lion is what a courtroom becomes at the moment of conviction: uktīn — "he proved it against him" — opens with the lion-sign, and someone is about to be eaten.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒌑	<b>grass</b> · U2 · <i>[u]</i> · plant, grass<br>Grass grows first — before anything else happens on a plot, the grass is already up. In the laws it is the same: before the verb gets anywhere, the grass-sign has already sprouted at its front.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒀉	<b>arm</b> · A2 · <i>[id/it/ed/et]</i> · veteran — A₂ gains [id/it/ed/et]: the dental family, both vowel colors<br>The arm does what law 1's verbs describe: it lays the charge and it carries out the sentence. When a law's verb opens on the arm, someone is being seized by it. From chapter 12 the arm covers its whole dental family in both vowel colors — it, ed, et: the perfect's ittadi, a name's ašarēd, the cheek-word lēt — one sign, four dress sizes of one sound.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒋳	<b>touch</b> · TAG · <i>[šum]</i> · to touch, strike; šumma's first half<br>Touch — every law begins by touching a hypothetical: if a man… The lightest touch of the stylus opens a whole world of consequence; that touch is this sign.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒉿	<b>ear</b> · PI · <i>[wa/wi]</i> · ear; the w Sumerian never wrote<br>An ear hears the witness — and every awīlum in every law is someone the court must hear. The man of the laws carries an ear in the middle of his name.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

The word for him ripens to its end on this sign.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

What is well-being — ṭūbum — if not being born into the world and kept whole in it? The birth-sign carries the king's promise to keep it so.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

𒀾	<b>curse</b> · AŠ2 · <i>[as]</i> · a curse in the lists<br>A curse, mid-sentence and defused: on the stele the bitter sign sits inside nasqā, "are choice" — the king praising his own words. Say as and note the irony; irony is memorable.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

Deeds first, blessing after: a fair order.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

The stele uses it to call its own words nasqā, "choice, picked out" — quality pressed from quantity.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

The syllable that sets the whole stele walking.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒀠	<b>hoe</b> · AL · <i>[al]</i> · the hoe<br>A hoe strikes the ground step after step, the way a durative verb keeps happening: illak, "he goes," itabbal, "he carries off" — both close on the hoe. Slow, repeated, thorough work.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

𒅀	<b>my</b> · IA · <i>[ia]</i> · i and a fused in one sign — the -ya of "my"<br>Two old friends — i and a — standing so close they became one sign, meaning my: what is mine stands that close to me. Write it whenever the writer claims something for himself.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103

𒁺	<b>go</b> · DU · <i>[ra]</i> · veteran — DU gains [ra₂]: the third sign of the bone-compound<br>The go-sign ends the bone-word — fitting, since nothing goes anywhere without bones. A foot-sign at the start, a foot-sign at the end, and the skeleton in between.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒈧	<b>kid</b> · MASZ2 · <i>[maš]</i> · the kid goat — and the interest on a loan: growth measured the herdsman's way<br>The kid in the ledger: every mina out on loan is a nanny goat, and MAŠ₂ counts what she bears. Where this sign appears, money is breeding.<br><i>KU₃.BABBAR u MAŠ₂.BI</i> — "the silver and its interest" — the repayment clause of a Sippar loan (urn:nabu:cdli:p257793:obverse:10, license: attribution)<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒂆	<b>shekel</b> · GIN2 · <i>[šiqlum]</i> · the shekel-sign — written GIN₂, spoken šiqlum: the weight silver moves in<br>The shekel: the small weight that prices a month of a man's work. Sixty of them make the mina; one of them, on this shelf's loan, is what a mina of silver breeds.<br><i>MAŠ₂ 1(diš) ma-na ▢ GIN₂</i> — "its interest: on the mina, a third of a shekel" — a Sippar rate (urn:nabu:cdli:p257793:obverse:2, license: attribution)<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒈹	<b>goddess</b> · INANNA · <i>[Ištar]</i> · the goddess's reed-bundle standard — written INANNA, spoken Ištar in Akkadian mouths<br>The goddess at the gate: her looped standard stood at the storehouse door, and the sign still stands wherever she is named — in hymns, in temples, and in the year-name of a Sippar loan.<br><i>MU E₂ {d}INANNA</i> — "Year: the temple of Inanna (…Immerum built)" — a year-name dating a loan (urn:nabu:cdli:p257793:reverse:1, license: attribution)<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒍝	<b>bead</b> · ZA · <i>[ṣa]</i> · veteran — ZA gains [ṣa]: uṣṣab, "it will grow" — interest's own syllable<br>A bead is wealth in its smallest unit — and uṣṣab is what wealth does in a loan contract: bead by bead, shekel by shekel, the interest grows. The pressed s is the sound of the count tightening.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒆠	<b>place</b> · KI · <i>[ki/qi]</i> · veteran — KI gains [ki/qi]: qibīma's opener — and the formulary's "from"<br>Place twice over: the ground a festival stands on when it is a syllable, and the place a loan comes FROM when the notary's old Sumerian does the talking. And pressed to its emphatic twin, qi, the place-sign opens qibīma, "speak!" — every letter in Babylon begins on it (chapter 12).<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒅈	<b>praise</b> · AR · <i>[ar]</i> · praise, glory in the lists; here the syllable of maḫar, "before"<br>Praise is standing before approving eyes — and the sign's big word, maḫar, is exactly that: standing before. An eye in the sign, an audience in the meaning.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒌫	<b>lap</b> · UR2 · <i>[ur]</i> · the lap — a body's base; foundations in the lists<br>The lap is where things rest and where they start. In this course it carries one unforgettable rest: the last syllable of līmur, "let him see his case" — the course's whole purpose, coming to rest on its last sign.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒆪	<b>seize</b> · KU · <i>[qu]</i> · veteran — KU gains [qu]: šūqurātim, "precious"<br>What is seized is held dear: press the k until it grips — qu — and you are inside šūqurātim, the king's own word for words worth keeping.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
𒀩	<b>statue</b> · ALAN · <i>[ṣalmum]</i> · the statue — a person's standing image; written ALAN, spoken ṣalmum<br>The statue is the person who stays. Hammurapi's laws end with an invitation to stand before HIS — ana maḫar ṣalmīya — and read. The sign is the king waiting in stone.<br>Edubba · edubba.ac · CC BY-SA 4.0; quoted lines carry their own licenses	edubba edubba-cuneiform-103
